parts.label: (b)
parts.stem:
Scientists compared features of the physiology of three groups of people who live at different altitudes. These people were selected from populations that have lived at these altitudes for many thousands of years.

The scientists took blood samples from people in each location and measured:

- the concentration of haemoglobin in the blood
- the percentage saturation of haemoglobin with oxygen in blood leaving the lungs
- the oxygen concentration in the blood leaving the lungs.

The results are shown in Table 3.1.

Table 3.1

| altitude / $\text{m}$ | location of group of people | mean haemoglobin concentration in blood / $\text{g }100\text{cm}^{-3}$ | mean percentage saturation of haemoglobin with oxygen in blood leaving the lungs | mean oxygen concentration in blood leaving the lungs / $\text{cm}^3 100\text{cm}^{-3}$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 100 (near sea level) | Peru | 15.3 | 97.0 | 21.1 |
| 3500 | East Africa mountains | 15.6 | 95.5 | 21.1 |
| 3750 - 4000 | Andes mountains | 19.1 | 92.0 | 22.0 |

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: Describe the changes in mean percentage saturation of haemoglobin with oxygen and the mean haemoglobin concentration in blood as altitude increases.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: With reference to Table 3.1, suggest how the people living at high altitude can have an oxygen concentration in blood leaving the lungs similar to that of the people living at sea level.
